A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-based token-sparsity work, renamed from ZipR1 to Sparsity Forcing. All pages, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original accuracy and token-retention results for three Qwen models across seven image and six video benchmarks in Tables 1–2.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons, ablations, robustness analyses, and latency/memory measurements in Tables 1–5 and Figures 3–6.

M1.justification: The GRPO/ZipVL framework remains, but v2 replaces v1's unconditional performance-plus-efficiency reward with a group-success gate: efficiency is rewarded only if at least one rollout answers correctly (Section 3.2, Equations 8–9). This is a localized objective refinement; the rename and expanded ZipVL description do not establish additional method changes.

E1.justification: The original thirteen benchmarks and Qwen calibration dataset remain. V2 adds HallusionBench for hallucination/visual-illusion evaluation and a subset of LLaVA-Video-178k for video calibration. These extend coverage within the existing image/video domains; adding the LLaVA backbone alone is not new task coverage.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates only full attention and ZipVL as comparators. V2 adds FastV and VisionZip to Qwen2.5 image comparisons; its LLaVA video comparisons also include MInference. Table 3 evaluates MOBA, post-trained ZipVL, and sharpness-loss baselines, while Figure 4 adds FlashAttention-2 resource comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds LLaVA-Video-7B evaluation, cross-benchmark averages, a FLOPs-equivalent ratio for MInference, budget/context-length sweeps, and controlled training-range/group-size experiments. The original training p range and inference p=0.975 remain. Newly disclosed Qwen frame/token counts do not establish changes to earlier settings, and the MLVU heading change from dev to M-avg does not establish a split change.

E4.justification: V1 contains no corresponding diagnostic experiments. V2 adds attention-mechanism ablations (Table 4), training-range and rollout-group-size ablations (Table 5), budget and context-length sensitivity tests, attention-map/layer-wise analyses, and low-budget HallusionBench robustness evaluation (Figures 3–6). These test component choices, adaptability, and preservation of visual evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's group-size ablation concerns GRPO training rollouts, not repeated experimental runs or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise many retained Qwen results. For example, Qwen2.5-VL-7B's proposed-method image ratio/MME is 24.3%/2320 in v1 and 24.7%/2286 in v2; full-attention MME also changes from 2337 to 2303. V2 additionally reports LLaVA, expanded baseline, ablation, robustness, and resource-use results. These are revised or new reports, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 introduces the mathematical group-success indicator and conditional reward in Equations 8–9. The common masking equations, attention-retention constraint, cited approximation bound, and GRPO objective remain substantively unchanged. Additional ZipVL equations largely formalize an existing component; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The central RL post-training contribution and thirteen-benchmark accuracy/sparsity claim remain. V1's 80% to 25% token retention and v2's 20% to 75% token reduction express the same claim. V2 adds quantified claims of up to 3× lower memory and 3.3× faster decoding to the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation beyond v1's brief performance discussion. It explains the all-incorrect-group reward failure, argues for grouped RL and layer-dependent sparsity, and interprets budget, context-length, and hallucination results. Its new limitations discussion identifies sequential multi-budget rollouts and incompatible KV-cache trajectories as barriers to batching and efficient training.

D1.justification: V2 supplies substantial previously absent implementation information: eight A100 GPUs, Adam with learning rate 1e-6, KL weight 0.04, training/evaluation frame and token counts, the 10k LLaVA calibration subset, and baseline block/budget settings. It also details ZipVL token selection and sequential rollout execution. These disclosures do not themselves establish changes to retained experiments.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated Related Work section covering methods including VisionZip, SparseVLM, SeerAttention, MMinference, and additional attention regularization work. It substantially develops its positioning against teacher-forced SFT, fixed sparsity patterns, and proxy objectives, and adds discussion of DPO and DAPO.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and method explanations are expanded. V1's compact Experiments section becomes separate Experimental Setup, Main Results, and Ablation Study and Discussion sections, alongside new Related Work and limitations text. The title and method terminology change throughout.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1 with a visual query and clearer rollout-group annotations, adds Figures 2–6, and introduces Tables 3–5. Tables 1–2 gain comparator rows, average columns, and a LLaVA model block. Multipanel plots, heatmaps, and text-wrapped displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V1 largely supports efficiency through accuracy/token-ratio tables against full attention and ZipVL. V2 substantially strengthens that evidence with broader baselines, measured resource use, diagnostic experiments, and implementation details. New reporting inconsistencies temper the gains: Table 3 lists Sparsity Forcing/Full averages as 70.0/70.2, contrary to the prose's 70.3/70.0, and Figure 4 labels the timing measurement as prefill despite the abstract's decoding-speedup claim. These errors weaken precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and reproducibility information.
